Dividing and Developing Land in Washington: Which Process You Are Actually In

8 min read·Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law

You own five acres outside town and want to carve off a piece for your daughter. Or you have a corner lot and a contractor who says you can put two small units behind the house. Or you are buying a building downtown and the seller mentions, late, that it needs to be condominiumized before the sale closes. Every one of these is a different legal process with different triggers, different timelines, and different people deciding, and the most expensive mistake is starting down the wrong one.

Washington puts the division of land under one chapter, chapter 58.17 RCW, and then exempts a surprising amount from it. The practical work at the start of a project is almost never about the merits. It is about correctly identifying which track you are on, because the track determines whether you are looking at a two-month administrative sign-off or a two-year public process.

The threshold question: how many lots, and are you making a new one

The statute draws its first line by counting. A subdivision is the division or redivision of land into five or more lots, tracts, parcels, sites, or divisions for the purpose of sale, lease, or transfer of ownership. A short subdivision is the same thing into four or fewer. That single number is what separates the long process from the short one.

The ceiling moves, though, and it moves locally. Cities and towns may raise the short subdivision maximum to nine lots by ordinance, and counties planning under the Growth Management Act may do the same inside urban growth areas. So the answer to whether your six-lot project is a short plat is not in the state statute. It is in the local code, and two neighboring jurisdictions can answer it differently.

The second question is whether you are creating a new lot at all. If you are not, chapter 58.17 RCW may not apply to you in the first place.

Boundary line adjustments: moving a line without making a lot

The exemption people most often need is in RCW 58.17.040(6). A division made for the purpose of alteration by adjusting boundary lines, between platted or unplatted lots or both, which does not create any additional lot, tract, parcel, site, or division, is exempt from the subdivision requirements.

There are two conditions buried in that sentence and both of them bite. No additional lot may be created, which means a boundary line adjustment moves lines between existing lots and never adds one. And the adjustment may not create a parcel with insufficient area and dimension to meet the minimum building site requirements. Shaving a strip off a nonconforming lot to help a neighbor can leave the first lot unbuildable, and a planner who notices will reject the application.

When it works, it is the cheapest tool in the chapter. It is also the one most often done casually between neighbors with a handshake and a surveyor, and then discovered years later by a title company that will not insure it.

Short plats and full subdivisions: the same project at two speeds

A short plat is the map or representation of a short subdivision, and in most jurisdictions it is an administrative decision. Staff review it, conditions attach, and it is recorded. There is usually no public hearing, which is why projects get designed to fit under the lot count.

A full subdivision runs in two stages. Preliminary plat approval is the decision that matters, because that is where the conditions are set: roads, utilities, stormwater, dedications, open space, frontage improvements. Final plat is the ministerial confirmation that you built or bonded what you were told to build. People focus on the final plat because it is the one that records, but by then every term has already been fixed.

The conditions are the real cost of a subdivision, and they are negotiated during preliminary review. That is the moment to have someone reading the local code against what staff is asking for.

Binding site plans: the commercial and condominium track

A binding site plan is a drawing to a scale specified by local ordinance that identifies streets, roads, improvements, utilities, and open spaces, carries the limitations and conditions the local government imposes, and contains provisions making development conform to the plan.

It matters because of two more exemptions. Divisions of land for industrial or commercial use are exempt from the subdivision chapter where the local government has approved a binding site plan, and so are divisions for the purpose of creating condominiums where a binding site plan has been approved. For a commercial project or a condominium, the binding site plan is often the entire land use path, and it replaces the plat rather than supplementing it.

What vests, and the exact moment it does

Under RCW 58.17.033 a proposed division of land is considered under the zoning and land use ordinances in effect on the land at the time a fully completed application is submitted. That is the vesting rule, and it is genuinely protective: once you are vested, a later code amendment does not reach back and change the rules on your project.

The weakness is in the phrase. The statute does not define a fully completed application. It says the requirements shall be defined by local ordinance. So the single most consequential date in a development project is governed by a local checklist, and an application that is missing one item on that checklist is not an application at all for vesting purposes.

This is where projects quietly lose. A developer submits in March, assumes they are vested, learns in June that the submission was incomplete, and by then the code has changed.

Accessory dwelling units, and what the state now requires

Washington has moved the floor under local ADU regulation. Under RCW 36.70A.681, cities and counties planning under the Growth Management Act must allow at least two accessory dwelling units on all lots in zoning districts within an urban growth area that allow single-family homes, in any of three configurations: one attached and one detached, two attached, or two detached.

The section also removes several of the tools local governments used to make ADUs impractical. A jurisdiction may not require the owner to live in the ADU or in another unit on the lot, which is the restriction that historically killed the most projects. Impact fees on an ADU may not exceed fifty percent of what would be imposed on the principal unit. Parking requirements are constrained near major transit stops and on smaller lots. And an ADU must be permitted on any lot meeting the minimum lot size for the principal unit.

What this does not do is override every other requirement. Setbacks, height, lot coverage, critical areas, and utility capacity still apply, and outside urban growth areas the picture is different.

Condominiumization: dividing the building rather than the ground

Converting a building into condominium units is not a subdivision of land in the ordinary sense, and it runs through a different body of law. Common interest communities in Washington are governed by the Washington Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act, chapter 64.90 RCW, with older condominiums still touching chapter 64.34 RCW.

Two things surprise owners. The first is the document load. A condominium is created by a recorded declaration and a survey map and plans, and a developer selling units owes a public offering statement with disclosure obligations attached to it. This is drafting work, not form-filling.

The second is that conversion of an occupied building carries tenant protections, including notice requirements, and those are not waivable by agreement with the buyer. If the building has tenants, the conversion timeline is driven by their rights, not by the closing date.

On the land use side, remember the exemption above: a division for the purpose of creating condominiums is exempt from the subdivision chapter where a binding site plan has been approved. Getting that approval is usually the local piece of a conversion.

Variances, conditional uses, and rezones

These are not division processes. They are relief from, or changes to, the rules that apply to a parcel, and they frequently run alongside a plat.

A variance asks to depart from a dimensional standard because of something about the property itself. A conditional use asks permission for a use the zone contemplates but does not permit outright. A rezone changes the classification and is legislative in character. Who decides each one, and whether that decision is a recommendation or a final determination, is set by the local ordinance and varies considerably.

The deadline to challenge any of them, once a decision issues, is short and unforgiving. That is its own subject, and I have written about it separately.

The Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area

If your property is in Clark, Klickitat, or Skamania County, there may be a second government in your permit.

The Columbia River Gorge Compact, ratified by Washington at chapter 43.97 RCW, created the Columbia River Gorge Commission as a bistate body with Oregon. The Commission reviews major development proposals and new residential construction within the scenic area, may disapprove development it finds inconsistent with the purposes of the compact, may disapprove local land use ordinances that do not conform, and may enact land use standards itself where a county does not.

The practical consequence is that a project there answers to the county code, the National Scenic Area Management Plan, and a commission whose standards are scenic, cultural, natural, and recreational rather than merely dimensional. Applications that would be routine a few miles east are not routine inside the boundary.

I hold bar admission in both Washington and Oregon, which matters here more than it does almost anywhere else in my practice, because the Gorge is administered across the state line by a single body.

Where this goes wrong

The wrong process. A project designed as a boundary line adjustment that actually creates a lot is not a boundary line adjustment, and the application will be rejected after the survey is paid for.

Vesting assumed rather than confirmed. The submission date only protects you if the application was complete under the local definition on that date.

Conditions accepted at preliminary plat without reading them. Frontage improvements and dedications imposed at that stage are the budget.

Discovering the Gorge boundary late. It does not follow county lines or the river bank, and the parcel either is inside it or is not.

Starting a condominium conversion with tenants in place and a fixed closing date.

Why this is lawyer work

Most of this is reading. Someone has to read the local code against the state statute, determine which process the project actually falls under, confirm what a complete application requires in that jurisdiction, and read the conditions before they are accepted rather than after. None of that is adversarial and most of it happens before anyone disagrees with anyone, which is exactly why it is cheap to do early and expensive to fix later.

About my practice

I am an independent attorney in downtown Spokane, at 601 W. 1st Ave., Suite 1400, admitted in Washington and in Oregon. Land use, subdivision, and development work is a regular part of my practice alongside real estate transactions and litigation, business and regulatory work, and civil litigation. I handle short plats, boundary line adjustments, subdivisions, binding site plans, condominium creation and conversion, ADU and infill projects, variances, conditional uses, and rezones, and I take Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area permitting, where my Oregon admission is directly useful.

If you are planning a division

The useful first conversation is short. What do you own, what do you want to end up with, and which jurisdiction is it in. From those three answers it is usually possible to say which process applies, roughly how long it takes, and what the real cost drivers are, before you have spent anything on survey or design.
